item.title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
item.description:
Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.
Authors: Kaden Zheng, Pratyusha Sharma
Tasks: Language Modeling
Code: https://github.com/KadenZheng/model-carving

item.title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
item.description:
Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.
Authors: Baihan Yang, Xin Lin, Yufan Wei, Baiang Li, Yuheng Liu, Juanxi Tian, Xiaohui Xie, Truong Nguyen
Tasks: Image generation, Image Matting, Text-to-Image Generation
Code: https://github.com/White-YC/pixelmatte

item.title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures
item.description:
Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.
Authors: Zhiyue Zhao, Mingyu Liu, Bolin Zhang, Liyang Li, Guangyu Huang, Canyu Zhao, Jinchuan Shi, Haokai Zhang, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
Tasks: Robotics, World Models
Code: https://github.com/aim-uofa/WorldReforge

item.title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
item.description:
Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
Authors: Tingting Liao, Mingjia Huo, Hao Li, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
Tasks: Robotics, Video generation, World Models
Code: https://github.com/TingtingLiao/SimPWM

item.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
item.description:
Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, model-driven context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~rightarrow~56\%), and Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
Authors: Alessio Devoto, Avinash Vem, Tara Safavi, Sanjay Kariyappa, Yu-Hsuan Tseng, Paul Furgale, Ricardo Silveira Cabral
Tasks: Harness Engineering, Long Context
Code: https://github.com/nvidia-nemo/labs-OO-Agents

item.title: OCRia-nano-1: Fast, Accurate CPU Parsing with 8.1M Parameters
item.description:
Recent vision-language models achieve strong document parsing accuracy but are optimized for server-grade GPUs. Existing CPU parsers still lag in accuracy, particularly in reconstructing tables and layout. We present OCRia-nano-1, an 8.1M-parameter document parsing pipeline optimized for CPU inference. The pipeline combines native PDF extraction with small models for OCR and document structure. LiteParse extracts available text and geometry, invokes OCR where needed, and supplies spatial features to LayoutNet, a joint table and layout reconstruction model. OCRia-nano-1 outperforms Indra and Marker on four of five benchmarks at comparable CPU throughput. On ParseBench-2, it scores 59.2, compared with 55.1 for Indra and 52.5 for Marker. It processes 27.8 pages per second on 16 vCPUs, twice the throughput of LiteParse’s default Tesseract configuration. Ablations show that joint table and layout reconstruction accounts for much of the accuracy gain, while larger OCR models provide only modest additional improvements. We release the model weights on Hugging Face under a modified OpenRAIL license, with LiteParse integration as an opt-in OCR backend.
Authors: Logan Markewich, Simon Suo
Tasks: Document Layout Analysis, OCR, Table Structure Recognition
Code: https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse

item.title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B
item.description:
Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B is the agentic release of the Ternary Bonsai 27B line. It keeps the Qwen3.8-27B hybrid-attention architecture and the ternary weight format of Bonsai 2, so it is still 1.76 bits per weight and 5.93 GB, against 53.8 GB for the FP16 model. This release targets long-horizon, tool-driven work.
Tasks: Agents, Coding Agents, Long-Horizon Agents
Code: https://github.com/prismml-eng/bonsai-demo

item.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
item.description:
Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.
Authors: Rui Sun, Junhua Huang, Luca Zancato, Md Mofijul Islam, Kai-Wei Chang
Tasks: Deep Research Agents
Code: https://github.com/uclanlp/OpenVLHarness

item.title: Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and Practical Multilingual Translation Models in the Wild
item.description:
Hy-MT3 is the third generation of the Hunyuan multilingual translation model family, including \textbf{Hy-MT3-1.8B}, \textbf{Hy-MT3-7B} and \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (MoE)}. Compared with Hy-MT2, Hy-MT3 translates \textbf{more accurately, more completely and more faithfully to user constraints}: on real-world scenario data, the share of samples with mistranslations is reduced by \textbf{43\%}, omissions or additions by \textbf{74\%}, and instruction-following errors by \textbf{40\%}, while language coverage is expanded from \textbf{38 to 102} languages. With only 3B activated parameters, \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models in non-thinking mode}, including flagship models such as Qwen3.8-Max, Kimi-K3.1-Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and approaches the strongest closed-source thinking models such as GPT-6.1-Sol and Gemini-4-Argon, while surpassing models that consume \textbf{more than 30$\times$} its inference compute. Beyond general translation, Hy-MT3 is optimized for two industrial scenarios. For \textbf{game localization}, built with high-quality game-domain data and a professional evaluation system from the Honor of Kings team, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B matches or outperforms strong closed-source models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro on all core metrics, and can be plugged into game development pipelines through an open-source toolchain. For \textbf{image translation}, Hy-MT3 improves context understanding and error correction to better tolerate OCR errors, achieving the best result among models of comparable size. Finally, we open-source \textbf{TransRubric}, a rubric-based automatic evaluation suite for translation, which outperforms other evaluation schemes on the WMT26 metrics shared task test set and is more stable with respect to human evaluation.
Authors: Mao Zheng, Zheng Li, Fangxu Liu, Tao Chen, Bingxin Qu, Bo Lv, Mingrui Sun, Hongyu Li, Hong Huang, Jinlong Song, Decheng Wu, Guanghua Yu
Tasks: Machine Translation
Code: https://github.com/tencent-hunyuan/hy-mt3

item.title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
item.description:
Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent
Authors: Lingwei Gu, Jimmy Lin
Tasks: Coding Agents, Long-Horizon Agents, Multi-Agent Systems
Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent

item.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
item.description:
Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT
Authors: Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang, Jinze Bai, BO WANG, Xiang Bai
Tasks: Language Modeling
Code: https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT

item.title: Improving and Expanding Video Editing Capabilities Without Videos
item.description:
Image editing models can follow a wide range of instructions, but video editing models still lag behind, limited in part by the difficulty of collecting paired source and edited videos. Is it possible to transfer advanced image editing capabilities to video editors without new paired videos? We introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which improves pretrained video editors and expands them to new editing tasks using an image editor. It enables efficient post-training with no architectural changes and no new videos, using only individual images. Our key idea is to let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an image as a one-frame video, with the image editor guiding the video editor's predictions at each denoising step. Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency. To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production, including action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. Our experiments across three different video editors show that I2VT improves existing editing capabilities and expands them to new tasks, and our models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.
Authors: Ji Xie, Yanhao Jia, Xiangpeng Yang, Martin Q. Ma, Sihan Xu, Erik Cambria, Louis-Philippe Morency
Tasks: Inverse Rendering, Video Editing, Video generation
Code: https://github.com/HorizonWind2004/i2v-transfer

item.title: Look Back: Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual World Models
item.description:
Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.
Authors: Jinwoo Kim, Toghrul Abbasov, Lucius E. J. Bynum, Aahlad Puli, Stephanie Milani, Hyunwoo Ryu, Seunghoon Hong, Kyunghyun Cho, Rajesh Ranganath
Tasks: Classic Reinforcement Learning, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, World Models
Code: https://github.com/ToghrulAbbasov19/look-back

item.title: Introducing the OpenResearch Intelligence Index
item.description:
The OpenResearch Intelligence Index is an open source composite index that tracks end-to-end autoresearch capabilities. Every model runs inside the full OpenResearch environment with its provider's own coding harness (Claude Code for Anthropic models, Codex for OpenAI models, and OpenCode for all others) and is scored on three areas: scientific knowledge (20 experimentation-heavy Terminal-Bench-Science tasks), post-training ability (6 PostTrainBench-based tasks that fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B and SmolLM2-360M on GSM8K, HumanEval, IFEval and BFCL), and literature relevancy and taste (45 PaperFindingBench queries grouped into 3 tasks). Each model makes 3 attempts per task, and the index is 0.4 Science + 0.4 PostTraining + 0.2 LiteratureRelevancy. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 sit on the cost-performance Pareto frontier.
Authors: Myles Anderson, Daniel Kim
Tasks: Auto-Research
Code: https://github.com/alphaxiv/openresearch

item.title: Non-penetrating World Models
item.description:
We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .
Authors: Yuhang Dai, Yinwei Wu, Ziyue Lin, Han Ji, Xingyi Yang
Tasks: World Models
Code: https://github.com/yuhangdai427/NoPeWorld

item.title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets
item.description:
Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.
Authors: Bohan Zeng, Kaixin Zhu, Yifan Yang, Dongge Yu, Zihao Wu, Yifan Dai, Zhou Liu, Junbo Niu, Xiaochen Ma, Shiran Ge, Zimo Meng, Junzhu Liang, Huanyao Zhang, JinHang Liu, Tianqi Xiao, Jinhao Zhang, Tianyi Bai, Zhixiong Zeng, Penghao Zhao, Yuanbo Peng, Key Zhang, Wentao Zhang
Tasks: Motion Generation, Video generation
Code: https://github.com/OpenDCAI/GameFactory-3A

item.title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
item.description:
A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.
Authors: Wongyun Yu, Honggeun Kim, Donguk Lee, Minchan Kim, Kyoung Whan Choe, Minsu Cho
Tasks: Reinforcement Learning, Robotics
Code: https://github.com/wongyun-yu/DexEngine

item.title: Agentic LongLive: Asynchronous Agentic Memory for Long Video Generation
item.description:
Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.
Authors: Shaoteng Liu, Shuai Yang, Wei Huang, Luozhou Wang, Song Han, Yukang Chen
Tasks: No-Reference Image Quality Assessment, Reinforcement Learning, Video generation
Code: https://github.com/NVlabs/LongLive

item.title: Building General-Purpose Robots Based on Embodied Foundation Model
item.description:
We are building embodied foundation models to capture and compress the world's most valuable data: continuous, high-fidelity physical interaction. By creating a direct feedback loop between model decisions and the body's lived experience, we enable generalizable intelligence that understands not just how the world works, but how to act effectively within it.
Tasks: Robotics
Code: https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/wall-x

item.title: PartAgent: Agentic 3D Part Segmentation via Expert Integration and Closed-Loop Refinement
item.description:
Segmenting a 3D object into semantically meaningful parts requires joint reasoning about geometric structure and semantic context. Pretrained 3D experts provide spatially grounded region proposals, while 2D experts provide semantic cues for identifying object parts. The challenge is to integrate these complementary capabilities into a framework that can both produce meaningful part segmentations and progressively refine them. We present PartAgent, a training-free agentic framework for 3D part segmentation built upon two complementary modules: (i) Structural-Semantic Expert Integration combines regions predicted by the 3D expert with multiview semantic evidence from the 2D expert through image-to-surface correspondences, constructing compositional part partitions at multiple granularities. (ii) Observation-Driven Closed-Loop Partition Refinement observes the current partition and its supporting evidence to select targeted inspection, evidence repair, composition, or reselection actions. It verifies proposed changes and uses the updated state and action outcomes to guide subsequent decisions. On PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT, PartAgent achieves 68.41 mIoU, outperforming the strongest competing method by 8.53 points. Across 3DCoMPaT200, PartNeXt, PartNetE, and PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartAgent achieves the highest mIoU on each dataset, averaging 69.36 across the four datasets, 7.28 points above the highest mean among competing methods.
Authors: Yang Cao, Zhe Zhu, Yiheng Zhang, Zhengqiang Zhang, Haoyuan Li, Le Wan, Dan Xu
Tasks: 3D semantic segmentation
Code: https://github.com/yangcaoai/PartAgent_Agent_for_3D_Part_Seg
